name: Socrates
summary: Socrates was an ancient Greek philosopher from Classical Athens, perhaps the first Western moral philosopher, and a major inspiration on his student Plato, who largely founded the tradition of Western philosophy.

facts.text: Socrates was sentenced to death in Athens after a jury found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the city's youth.
facts.context: Socrates turns questioning into a real risk: asking uncomfortable questions can threaten people who depend on obedience.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica describes Socrates' trial, charges, conviction, and death sentence in Athens.

facts.text: Socrates was an ancient Greek philosopher from Classical Athens, perhaps the first Western moral philosopher, and a major inspiration on his student Plato, who largely founded the tradition of Western philosophy.
facts.context: Socrates's background gives readers a concrete entry point into Philosophy, Ethics & Religion.

facts.text: An enigmatic figure, Socrates authored no texts and is known mainly through the posthumous accounts of classical writers, particularly his students Plato and Xenophon.
facts.context: Socrates's challenge makes the card about pressure and choice, not just fame.

facts.text: These accounts are written as dialogues, in which Socrates and his interlocutors examine a subject in the style of question and answer; they gave rise to the Socratic dialogue literary genre.
facts.context: Socrates's turning point shows how one moment can redirect a public life.

facts.text: Contradictory accounts of Socrates make a reconstruction of his philosophy nearly impossible, a situation known as the Socratic problem.
facts.context: Socrates's contribution helps explain why this profile belongs in the People Library.

facts.text: Socrates was a polarizing figure in Athenian society.
facts.context: Socrates's influence connects one short Fact to a wider historical ripple.
